anchors.applies_other: functional-requirement (per notation: Agile story, use-case sea/fish, prose requirement)
anchors.definition: Testable conditions of satisfaction for a functional requirement (story) — the check that says "done and correct." Written in Gherkin form so they're unambiguous and verifiable:
anchors.name: Acceptance Criteria (Given/When/Then)

anchors.applies_other: architecture area · building blocks · decision records
anchors.definition: The template for communicating and documenting software architecture, by Dr. Peter Hruschka & Dr. Gernot Starke (template V9, July 2025; https://arc42.org, docs at https://docs.arc42.org). Twelve sections; this wiki shares sections 1–3 and 9–12 with req42 (the commons area) and implements the architecture-only sections 4–8 as one content type each.
anchors.name: arc42

anchors.definition: Quality criteria for a user story (complements the User-Story Format shape).
anchors.name: INVEST

anchors.definition: Markdown Any Decision Records — the record format for a decision record (DR-NNN). MADR started as "Markdown Architectural Decision Records" and extends Michael Nygard's Context / Decision / Consequences with an explicit comparison of options. Reference: https://adr.github.io/madr/ (MADR 4.x).
anchors.name: MADR

anchors.definition: The shared meaning of the priority field used across features, use cases, stories, and quality requirements. One definition, cited everywhere.
anchors.name: MoSCoW

anchors.definition: A lightweight goal frame — the minimal viable alternative to SMART when full rigor is unwarranted or premature. Three parts:
anchors.name: PAM

anchors.definition: The shape of the scenario on every quality requirement, after the arc42 quality model Q42 (quality.arc42.org): a quality need, tagged with its Q42 dimensions and made concrete and testable by one scenario. Q42 is the pragmatic choice here; the wiki never calls these "ATAM scenarios".
anchors.name: Q42

anchors.definition: The pragmatic, agile, just-in-time framework for requirements documentation and communication, by Dr. Peter Hruschka & Markus Meuten (CC BY-SA 4.0). It is the umbrella methodical reference for this vault: our content types are essentially req42's sections, and the smaller anchors (SMART, PAM, INVEST, MoSCoW, User-Story Format) are standards req42 uses inside those sections. Fuller reading copy: docs/req42/. Canonical source: https://github.com/Hruschka/req42-framework.
anchors.name: req42

anchors.definition: A goal-framing standard. Use when a goal warrants full rigor; for a lighter frame use PAM.
anchors.name: SMART

anchors.applies_other: functional requirements (req42 section 04) · epics · features · user-stories
anchors.definition: A technique (Jeff Patton) for arranging the functional requirements (req42 block 04) as a 2-D map instead of a flat, context-free backlog list — so you can explain the whole system, find gaps, and slice releases. It is the way req42 recommends maintaining the functional-requirements hierarchy (Hruschka cites Patton).
anchors.name: Story Mapping

anchors.definition: The canonical shape of a user story. Quality of a story is judged separately by INVEST; priority by MoSCoW.
anchors.name: User-Story Format

universal_fields.name: title

projections.name: addressed-by
projections.summary: The inverse of rel-drivers on a goal, use case, functional requirement, quality requirement or constraint: which decisions, building blocks, solution strategies, deployment nodes and crosscutting concepts answer it.

projections.name: backlog-ranking
projections.summary: What req42 still calls the Product Backlog: the ranked, linear reading of the hierarchy — by release, then priority, then order. Declared here so that the word "backlog" has exactly one meaning in this wiki: a view, never a drawer.

projections.name: bb-tree
projections.summary: The levels of the Building Block View from rel-parent: level 1 under the system, then each block's children. A block whose parent is empty, a context page or missing counts as level 1, so nothing drops out of the view.

projections.name: context-diagram
projections.summary: Projected from edges, never stored: EIF flows for systems, STK provides / receives for human roles. Deprecated interfaces are drawn nowhere. "No drift by construction" — inspect only checks that the edges are consistent.

projections.name: deployment-diagram
projections.summary: Nodes nested by rel-parent, the blocks they host inside them, rel-connects as edges labelled with the protocol. One diagram of all states: current plain, planned and target dashed, outdated grey, a dotted edge to the successor. Never stored.

projections.name: entity-diagram
projections.summary: Classes are the stereotyped domain terms. Edges come from rel-relationships and sum-type parents.

projections.name: goal-coverage
projections.summary: Objectives × epics, from rel-goal. An objective no epic serves is a gap; a backbone epic with goal: [] is a rule violation (rule-fr-traces-to-goal).

projections.name: goal-tree
projections.summary: Vision → objectives from rel-parent; the goal/epic map on the functional- requirements page extends it one level down through rel-goal.

projections.name: governed-by
projections.summary: The inverse of rel-applies-to: which crosscutting concepts a block or node follows. Concepts with an empty applies-to govern the whole system and are listed on the concepts view, not on every page.

projections.name: sequence-diagram
projections.summary: One participant per distinct from / to, in order of first appearance (stakeholders as actors), one arrow per step. Never stored. Steps between blocks are checked against rel-uses (rule-runtime-matches-uses).

projections.name: story-map
projections.summary: Patton's 2-D map over Agile FRs: backbone = epics in order, ribs = features and stories by priority, swim-lanes = release. Fully derivable from the fields above, so it is never hand-authored (Story Mapping). Other notations remain in the unified FR list and are not forced into this projection. One exception: a sea- or fish-level use case that Agile features or stories name as parent: appears as a root beside the epics, with those children under it (DR-038 amendment).

projections.name: terminology-graph
projections.summary: All domain terms are core nodes. Filter the graph by edge kind to inspect links or model structure.

projections.name: whitebox
projections.summary: A block's inner structure: its children as boxes, their rel-uses dependencies as arrows, external interfaces they use as neighbour boxes. Never stored.

relations.meaning: The roles that take part in a process.

edges.note: this record changes some points of the target, which stays in force

relations.meaning: A later decision that changes part of an earlier one. The earlier record stays accepted; its readers follow the inverse, which the dashboard projects.
The blocks and nodes a crosscutting concept governs. Empty means the whole system. The inverse is projected onto their pages (proj-governed-by).

edges.note: PAM Advantage: who gets the benefit

relations.meaning: Who a goal is for. Feeds the stakeholder matrix report; not drawn anywhere yet.

edges.note: set at capture; structures the requirements (FR-005)

relations.meaning: "This requirement concerns that building block." Assignment, not ownership and not traceability: it structures the requirements by the parts of the system they apply to, and is set when the requirement is captured. The traceability statement runs the other way, as the building block's drivers; both may connect the same pair, because they say different things (FR-005, DR-038).

edges.note: structured entries {to, protocol?, note?}, stored on the initiating side

relations.meaning: A channel between nodes, or to an external system, labelled with its protocol in the proj-deployment-diagram.

"This decision or building block rests on that requirement." The bridge from architecture to requirements, deliberately lightweight: optional, no coverage rule. The inverse, addressed by, is projected onto the requirement pages (proj-addressed-by). On a decision record it is the linked form of MADR's "Decision Drivers"; the body section keeps the prose.

edges.note: [] is an explicit enabler (lane platform/display), not a gap — unless the item is backbone

relations.meaning: "This requirement serves that goal." Source of the proj-goal-coverage matrix (DR-018). A backbone epic or feature with goal: [] is a rule violation; a platform item with goal: [] is an enabler.
The mapping of software to infrastructure: the building blocks deployed on a node.
The reverse of rel-sources, maintained by capture. Keeps the historical name "ingested" on purpose (the workflow was renamed to capture, the field was not).

edges.note: a stakeholder link only, no literal; empty means not yet clear who can answer

relations.meaning: The stakeholder an Issue's question is addressed to: the one whose answer resolves it. Usually a stakeholder group, not a person. There is no due date: the wiki is not a project management tool. Counterpart of rel-raised-by, which says who put the question on the table.

edges.note: story → feature → epic; a feature or story may also name a sea- or fish-level use case (DR-038 amendment); several parents make it a graph, the dashboard draws the first (DR-012)

relations.meaning: The one stakeholder whose goal a Cockburn use-case requirement is. Supporting actors stay prose links. A stakeholder with no inbound primary-actor and no FR mention is a coverage gap (inspect).

edges.note: or the literal agent — the one field that is link-or-literal

relations.meaning: Who put the question on the table. The literal agent is allowed because most Issues come out of capture, not from a stakeholder.
The requirement or process a runtime scenario carries out; the bridge from the runtime view back to the requirements, so the flow is not written twice.

relations.meaning: The one symmetric relation. Because it is symmetric, the relations linter may repair a missing back-link on its own (tiers 1–2 of relations.md); every other relation is directed and its reverse is projected or capture-maintained.

relations.meaning: The one system under discussion of a Cockburn use-case requirement: either a building block at any level, or the context when the use case covers the whole system. The field is required and carries exactly one link in total; the two target types are alternatives, not two separate scopes. No whole-system building-block page is needed merely to provide a scope target.
The decision records that shaped an architecture page (field decisions). Together with rel-drivers it answers "why is this block like this?".

edges.note: empty sources and no [!assumption] ⇒ inspect raises an Issue

relations.meaning: Provenance: every derived claim links the source it came from. The reverse list, rel-ingested-pages, is written by the capture workflow (step 5), not by the linter — a directed relation whose inverse happens to be stored.

edges.note: structured entries {from, to, message, note?}, in order
drawn as an actor

relations.meaning: The ordered interactions of a runtime scenario. Each entry carries both ends and the message, like rel-relationships. Read by proj-sequence-diagram.

replaced by its successor; status unchanged, state outdated once gone
replaced by its successor; status unchanged, state outdated once gone
replaced by its successor; status unchanged, state outdated once gone
replaced by its successor; status unchanged, state outdated once gone
replaced by its successor; status unchanged, state outdated once gone

relations.meaning: Points from a replaced decision to its successor. Unlike rel-amends it is stored on the old record, which is deprecated at the same time. On an architecture page it links the page to the one that replaces it; the old page keeps its status, since a correct description of a past element stays correct, and its state becomes outdated once the element is gone.

edges.note: a neighbour system, drawn outside the white box

relations.meaning: A static dependency: this block needs that block or that external system. The arrows of the proj-whitebox and of the level-1 overview.

rules.check: goal is non-empty, or lane is platform | display (an explicit enabler), or the first parent is a use case with non-empty goal (the feature serves the use case's goals)
rules.name: fr-traces-to-goal
rules.summary: Advisory: raise an ISS-NNN, never fill goal in. Goal coverage (proj-goal-coverage) is only as good as this edge.

rules.check: Review terms that share a title or alias within one bounded context.
rules.name: one-term-per-meaning
rules.summary: Review terms that share a title or alias within one bounded context.

rules.check: if A lists B in related, B lists A in related
rules.name: related-reciprocal
rules.summary: Mechanical and safe: the relation is symmetric by declaration (rel-related), so the missing side is added without asking.

rules.check: for each step whose from and to are both building blocks, from (or a parent: ancestor of it) lists to (or an ancestor of to) in uses:
rules.name: runtime-matches-uses
rules.source: arc42 runtime and building-block view consistency
rules.summary: Advisory: capture and inspect ask the human whether the step or the uses: edge is wrong. Never edits either.

rules.check: pages of different types with the same kebab slug-suffix or identical title link each other in related
rules.name: same-slug-same-concept
rules.summary: A domain term and the building block that implements it can share a name. Capture links the two views of that concept.

rules.check: Terms with attributes, relationships or a parent carry a stereotype. Relationship targets are stereotyped. Only entities have a source of truth or identifier attributes.
rules.name: structure-needs-stereotype
rules.summary: Terms with attributes, relationships or a parent carry a stereotype. Relationship targets are stereotyped. Only entities have a source of truth or identifier attributes.
